19667-an-essay-on-the-influence-of-tobac:
Few habits drew more ink in the nineteenth century than tobacco. An Essay on the Influence of Tobacco upon Life and Health argues the case against it. The writer pictures the user warping a form made with symmetry and elegance. In his words, the smoker can turn himself into something hideous. The tone is moral as much as medical.

Anti-tobacco tracts mixed health claims, religion, and disgust. They warned readers long before modern cancer studies existed. Some of their claims were guesswork dressed as fact. Others pointed, early, at real harms. The essay is a record of how reformers argued. It shows the sermon style that health campaigns once used.
19747-where-the-sun-swings-north:
Barrett Willoughby set Where the Sun Swings North in Alaska, and published it in 1922. It opens in a rough office at a northern trading post. A man with expert eyes closes his ledger with relief. He claps his hands, and a curtain at the side doorway draws aside. A small brown feminine hand appears through it. The scene promises frontier business and romance together.

Willoughby knew Alaska from years of living and working there. Her novels mixed trading-post fact with adventure plots. Gold, weather, and isolation set the terms for her characters. Northern fiction sold well in the 1920s. This book shows why readers trusted her detail. The ledger and the curtain sum up her two worlds.
19921-prehistoric-textile-art-of-eastern:
William H. Holmes studied prehistoric textile art of the eastern United States. The Bureau of Ethnology asked him about 1890 to prepare the study. It accompanied Cyrus Thomas's final report on mound explorations. The papers treat aboriginal arts shown by recovered relics. Textiles survive poorly, so Holmes worked from fragments and impressions. Cloth pressed into clay and copper kept its patterns after the fibers rotted.

Ancient Eastern weavers used twining, braiding, and early loom work. Holmes classified their techniques from the scraps that remained. His drawings reconstructed fabrics no eye had seen whole for centuries. The study appeared in the Bureau's Thirteenth Annual Report. It founded the study of prehistoric American textiles. Modern analysts still build on Holmes's categories.
20059-left-on-the-labrador-a-tale-of-adv:
Dillon Wallace wrote Left on the Labrador, a tale of adventure down north. Wallace knew the Labrador wilds from his own hard trips there. The book opens with verse on a life of storms and calms. Thorns sit among flowers, the poem says, yet we should stay glad as we can.

Inside, young travelers face cold, hunger, and vast empty country. Wallace writes of coasts and woods that few readers of his day had seen. The tale gives boys a true taste of the far north. Grit and teamwork matter more here than luck or ease.
20135-the-angel-of-death:
The Angel of Death comes from Swedish, in a translation printed at New York. It tells of Johan, a poet and preacher born in Dalarne in 1779. His father, a captain, led the Dalecarlia regiment in Sweden. Johan was one of a large family raised on modest means.

A poet-preacher's life in old Sweden forms the core of the tale. Faith, verse, and duty shape his path from a soldier's home. The angel of death in the title hangs over the story's mood. Readers get a sober life tale with strong religious feeling throughout.
20251-christmas-comes-but-once-a-year-sh:
Christmas Comes But Once a Year shows what Mr. Brown did at that season. Very cold, very bleak weather opens the tale in brisk strokes. The thermometer and snow fall fast as Christmas nears. Eggs and suet, by contrast, rise faster in price each day.

Everyone wishes everyone else a merry Christmas and a happy new year. Behind that cheer sit tight purses and hard choices for Brown. Holiday tales often test a clerk's purse against his family's hopes. Readers get a comic, touching slice of Victorian Christmas on a budget.
20294-a-handbook-of-health:
Woods Hutchinson published A Handbook of Health in 1911, a guide to the human body. He compares the body to an automobile before a long ride. A wise driver first learns how that car is built and fueled. He learns its gears, its tires, and how to cure engine troubles.

So, too, should a person learn the workings of their own frame. Hutchinson, a doctor, writes in bright, plain, friendly terms throughout. Food, air, exercise, and rest all get clear, practical chapters. Readers get Edwardian health advice that still reads fresh and direct.
20305-marion-s-faith:
Marion's Faith, from 1886, is a novel of army life on the western frontier. A young officer jokes about paying for the clothes he wears. He glances down at his well-worn uniform as he speaks lightly. He prays they will be sent to reinforce Crook in Sioux country.

Out there, he says, no new uniforms are needed for scouting work. Crook, the Gray Fox, led troops in hard campaigns against the Sioux. Marion's faith will be tested by distance, danger, and duty alike. Readers get a frontier romance with a strong religious heart.
20309-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-in-:
Laura Lee Hope published Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue in the Sunny South in 1921. Bunny and Sue play in their backyard after a heavy snow storm. They build a big man of snow in the clean, fallen snow. Their mother let them out once the weather grew warm enough.

From snow at home, the tale soon turns toward the sunny south. Travel gives the Brown children new sights, foods, and friends. Each book in the series mixes mild mishaps with safe fun. Young readers get a warm trip south with two cheerful guides.
20388-report-of-the-railway-department-o:
When railways were new, the Board of Trade's Railway Department reported to Parliament on the lines being planned. This report weighs rival schemes for routes linking Oxford with the Midlands. Each line promised trade, speed, and profit for its backers.

One scheme ran from Oxford to Worcester and Wolverhampton, promoted by an independent company. It worked in connection with the Great Western Company. Together with the Oxford and Rugby line it formed one plan, set against competing routes. The report shows how Victorian Britain argued over steel, money, and maps before a single rail was laid.
20636-the-military-journals-of-two-priva:
The Military Journals of Two Private Soldiers presents the diaries of common soldiers from 1758 to 1775. One journal covers the French and Indian War, and the other reaches toward the Revolution. Private soldiers rarely left records, which makes these pages precious.

The editor believed the journals might interest American readers. They exhibit the everyday life of a common soldier in those wars which led to the founding of the republic. He yielded, he says, to the urging of friends and to his own judgment in printing them. Camps, marches, hunger, and skirmishes fill the plain daily entries.
20745-an-outcast-or-virtue-and-faith:
Virtue and Faith, sold also as An Outcast, opens with a bold claim about reform writing. The author says timid books hide real evils and lose all force. A cure, the preface argues, needs the cause shown plainly to the public eye.

That pledge shapes a tale of a cast-out figure tested by a harsh world. Vice, poverty, and faith pull at the lead figure across the plot. The book belongs to the earnest reform fiction of its century. Readers can see how such novels tried to move hearts and change laws at the same time, with story as their chief tool.
20795-the-cricket-on-the-hearth:
A kettle and a cricket open Charles Dickens's The Cricket on the Hearth, in this 1905 text. The kettle, one voice swears, began a full five minutes before the cricket sang. Mrs. Peerybingle's word rules the house, so the point needs care.

Dickens calls this tale a fairy tale of home, and the Peerybingles fill it with warmth. A blind girl, a gruff toymaker, and a test of trust deepen the plot. The cricket stands for hearth luck and kind hearts. Among Dickens's Christmas books, this one is the coziest, built for fireside reading in the dark of the year.
20913-a-woman-s-journey-through-the-phil:
Church and convento at Dumaguete, an old fort at Misamis, and bands that serenade guests fill the plates. Her Philippines travel book, from 1907, rides a cable ship that laid wire at sea. Markets, rivers, and street scenes crowd its photo list.

The traveller here sailed where cables linked far islands. She writes of towns, folk, and work with a keen, curious eye. Laying cable from native schooners shows the hard craft below deck talk. The book freezes the Philippines under early American rule, in vivid, first-hand travel prose. Few travel books of its day match its close, curious view of island life at work.
20941-american-lutheranism-volume-1-earl:
American Lutheranism, says F. Bente, is just Lutheranism in America, no fresh brand of faith. Doctrine, he holds, stays the same the world over, as does the church. Volume one treats the early history and the Tennessee Synod in that light.

Bente, a Missouri Synod scholar, traces Lutheran roots from colonial days onward. Synods, schools, doctrine fights, and pioneers fill his careful record. He writes to fix the facts of a church oft split by tongue and place. Church historians still use his volumes, written from inside the fold with a clerk's care for names, dates, and acts.
21037-the-cock-house-at-fellsgarth:
New boys tumble headlong into public school life in The Cock-House at Fellsgarth, and pay for it. Pocket money, hamper goods, and luckless freshmen all fall to old rule, Reed writes. Custom, immemorial and stern, owns the first hard days at school.

Fellsgarth's houses, games, feuds, and codes fill Reed's tale of school honour. The cock-house, top house of the school, sets the tone boys must meet. Reed knew this world from The Boy's Own Paper's vast readership. His Fellsgarth tales still stand as models of the classic British school story, brisk and fair.
21128-twenty-years-of-congress-vol-1-fro:
James G. Blaine, one of the most powerful Republicans of his age, published this political history in 1884. Volume One reviews the events that led to the political revolution of 1860, then follows Congress from Lincoln toward Garfield. Blaine wrote as a participant: he served in the House and Senate through these years.

Portraits of Lincoln, Sumner, Douglas, Stevens, and other leaders front the chapters. Blaine explains slavery politics, the Civil War Congresses, and Reconstruction from a Republican statesman's view. Statistical appendices back the narrative. The book remains a primary source for how Blaine's generation understood its own revolution in government.
21353-civics-and-health:
William H. Allen, secretary of the Bureau of Municipal Research, published Civics and Health with Ginn and Company in 1909. MIT biologist William T. Sedgwick wrote the introduction. Its frontispiece quote from Louis Agassiz claims a natural law is as sacred as a moral principle. Allen links the two in city government and schools.

Allen had led work on the physical welfare of New York school children. The book argues that health is a civic duty, not only a private one. Clean water, school inspection, and honest administration belong to one subject. It belongs to the Progressive era's push to run cities on science and records rather than patronage.
21397-manco-the-peruvian-chief-or-an-eng:
Peru, the old land of the Incas, is the scene of W. H. G. Kingston's Manco, the Peruvian Chief. An English family lives there under the shadow of Spanish rule. They watch a grand show from their country house as the tale begins.

The family is drawn into helping Manco, an Inca chief, flee the Spaniards. Kingston stresses how harshly Spain ground down the native tribes. A long trek overland brings danger from soldiers, snakes, bad bridges, and river rafts. Written in 1853, the book is among Kingston's first, and its style is already clean and sure.
21410-the-isle-of-pines-1668-and-an-essa:
Henry Neville's The Isle of Pines, first issued in 1668, tells of a castaway and four women on a lone island. The ship was bound for the East Indies when it was wrecked near a far coast. All aboard drowned save those five, one of the women being a Black servant.

The 1920 Boston edition pairs the tale with a long study by Worthington Chauncey Ford. Ford traces the Dowse copies and the Dutch, French, Italian, and German printings. He weighs who wrote the tale and how Defoe may have used it. Book lovers get both a strange early tale and its full print history.
21477-mark-seaworth:
Mark Seaworth searches for his sister and for his own true name in W. H. G. Kingston's Mark Seaworth. A calm ocean, smooth as a mirror under a blue sky, opens the tale. Moonlight makes a broad silver path across the dark sea in its early scenes.

Kingston tells the hunt through rich local detail and clean, fine English. The book was the first of his works put online by its modern editors. They praise it as a shining case of good writing throughout. Quests, sea travel, and slow reveals of kinship carry a story that many readers count among his best.
21500-memoirs-of-the-court-of-queen-eliz:
Lucy Aikin published her Memoirs of the Court of Queen Elizabeth in two volumes in 1818. Her plan covers Elizabeth's private life from birth onward. It adds the home history of the reign and lives of the great noble families.

Anecdotes of famed courtiers fill the pages, with notes on manners, thought, and letters. A front picture shows Elizabeth in the dress she wore to give thanks for the Armada's defeat. Aikin saw that England had many fine histories but few of this close, domestic kind. Her book still serves readers who want the court from inside.
21560-papers-on-health:
Professor Kirk's Papers on Health, first spread over eleven volumes, is here cut to one by his son Edward. The 1904 edition updates the doctor's advice where surgery and practice had moved on. Readers who want the raw text are sent to the full original set.

Kirk treats sore throats, fevers, diet, and the care of the body at home. Some practices he attacked had died out by the time of this edition. The editor owns each change as his own work and choice. The book preserves a famed Victorian health guide, whose plain rules reached many homes.
21790-the-dance-of-death:
Death comes for pope and peasant alike in Hans Holbein's famous Dance of Death. This 1903 edition adds a note by Austin Dobson. The earliest edition appeared at Lyons in 1538, a small quarto with forty-one cuts. Each picture carries a text from the Latin Bible above it. A long French preface addressed a noble abbess of Lyons, head of a house of wealthy ladies.

Holbein's woodcuts show skeletons leading away every rank of life, from the highest to the lowest. The images are elegant, sharp, and quietly funny about human pride. Dobson's introduction traces the book's strange publication history. Few picture books have been copied so often or remembered so long. This edition puts the classic within easy reach.
21895-the-old-coast-road-from-boston-to-:
The shore road from Boston to Plymouth is walked town by town in Agnes Edwards's The Old Coast Road, published in 1920. Edwards likens a city's story to a layer cake: cut down and every slice shows all the layers. Her road passes Dorchester Heights, Milton and the Blue Hills, and shipbuilding Quincy, home of the Adams houses. Louis H. Ruyl's illustrations and a map of the South Shore guide the eye.

Weymouth's romance, churchly Hingham with its Old Ship Meeting-House, and Cohasset's ledges follow in turn. Marshfield brings Daniel Webster's home, and Duxbury and Kingston lead at last to Plymouth. The book mixes travel, history, and local lore in a chatty voice. It is an armchair tour of old Massachusetts, made when the road still belonged to horses and memory.
21905-a-guide-for-the-religious-instruct:
Teachers of Jewish youth get a full course of faith in Isaac Reggio's Guide. M. H. Picciotto Englished it from the Italian in 1855. Reggio, rabbi and professor at Gorizia, was famed in the Hebrew literary world as scholar, philosopher, and elegant writer. His course moves in order: God, man, natural religion, and the need for revelation.

Numbered sections argue God's existence and attributes, then man's faculties, free will, conscience, and immortal soul. Natural religion is honored, then shown to fall short without revealed religion. The plan is rational and orderly, in the spirit of the Jewish Enlightenment. It shows how one great scholar thought the young should be taught to reason about their faith.
21999-the-wind-bloweth:
Ireland's passing world is mourned and sung in Donn Byrne's The Wind Bloweth, published in 1922 with illustrations by George Bellows. In his dedication, written as a prayer, Byrne says he chased the unbearable ache that is the mainspring of humanity. He worked through a race he knew best. They believe in Christ yet still believe in the little people of the hills. They love their own land, yet wander the wide world. He feared the Gaelic tongue itself was dying as he wrote.

Byrne had won readers with Messer Marco Polo, a tale of the East. Here he turns home to Ireland, to battle-loving people who always fall and always sing. The prose is lush and musical. The book catches a culture at the moment of its vanishing, and holds it beautifully.
22132-giants-on-the-earth:
Captain S. P. Meek wrote Giants on the Earth, a science fiction tale of revolt against alien masters. Giants from Jupiter rule the Earth through their viceroy, Glavour. The Jovians' huge bodies, bred for their planet's heavy gravity, dwarf ordinary humans. Earth lies under their yoke, waiting for a leader.

That leader is Damis, called the Nepthalim, who rallies Earth to spirited revolt. Meek builds his pulp plot on a simple contrast: giant tyrants, small rebels. Battles and escapes follow in the magazine style of the early 1930s. Meek, a serving army officer, wrote much early science fiction, and this tale shows the field in its raw, energetic youth.
22292-glory-of-youth:
Temple Bailey, one of America's most popular romantic novelists, wrote Glory of Youth as a story of young love and old houses. Miss Matthews, the companion, is glad to take the rooms just as they are. She was delighted to be asked to stay after mother died, the heroine explains. She loves the old things: the mahogany, the banjo clock, the embroidered peacocks, and the Venetian heirlooms from Dad's family.

Bailey sets that cherished household against the claims of youth and romance. Her heroines are modern girls with old-fashioned hearts, and her houses are characters too. The book has the gloss of the magazine fiction Bailey supplied by the shelf. It is sentiment, neatly made.
22424-frank-merriwell-down-south:
Frank Merriwell Down South, dated 1903, sends the famous schoolboy hero traveling. A dying man gives Frank the book's great clue at the start. Treasure lies in Mexico's Sierra Madre range, he says.

The spot stands one hundred twenty-five miles west of Zacatecas. Across a blue chasm, its towers and turrets glisten in sunshine. The dying man calls it a beautiful, dazzling dream. Frank Merriwell was the model hero of American dime novels. He was honest, athletic, and quick in every crisis. This southern adventure adds lost treasure to his usual tests. Readers get brisk period storytelling built for eager boys.
22500-the-works-of-william-hogarth-in-a-:
The Works of William Hogarth presents the great artist's engravings in series. Descriptions accompany the plates so readers can study each scene. A biographical search opens the inquiry into Hogarth's family.

His father's school stood in 1712 in the parish of St. Giles. In that parish register, searchers hoped to find his death recorded. The register was searched, the account says, to no purpose. Such detective work frames the edition's care for facts. Hogarth's own prints need less help: they satirize English life brilliantly. Rakes, elections, and marriages unfold panel by panel in his lines. Readers get both the pictures and period commentary. Together they preserve Georgian England laughing at itself.
22735-king-of-the-jews-a-story-of-christ:
William T. Stead adapted King of the Jews from the Oberammergau Passion Play, telling the story of Christ's last days on earth; the book appeared in 1900. Stead, the famous campaigning journalist, shaped the Bavarian villagers' play into a narrative for English readers who would never see the original.

The sample shows the entry into Jerusalem: amid the jubilant crowd, Jesus appeared in a long gray garment with a flowing robe cast over it. His face was calm and thoughtful. Sun had darkened his long black hair and beard. He rode on a colt that looked nearly too small to bear his weight. Stead writes reverently and vividly, scene by scene. The book carried the Passion Play's fame around the English-speaking world.
22764-on-the-origin-of-species-by-means-:
Charles Darwin wrote On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, the 1859 book that changed biology forever. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Darwin argues that species arise from earlier species, shaped over ages by natural selection acting on small variations, as breeders shape pigeons and dogs.

His introduction recalls the voyage of the Beagle. Facts about the distribution of South America's inhabitants first struck him there. So did the relations of present to past life on that continent. Those facts, he writes, seemed to throw light on the origin of species. One great philosopher had called that problem the mystery of mysteries. The book that grew from them marshals geology, breeding, and island life into one vast argument. No summary can replace reading the argument itself, still lucid and bold.
23129-the-young-voyageurs-boy-hunters-in:
Thomas Mayne Reid outfits his hunters in The Young Voyageurs, boy hunters in the North. A vast journey it will be, the narrator warns. It will cost many thousand miles of travel. No train, steamboat, stagecoach, or even a horse will carry them, the narrator warns. No hotel board or roadside inn waits along their route either.

Reid's boys travel by canoe and snowshoe through the fur country, hunting to eat and learning the North animal by animal. His books mixed adventure with real natural history, and young readers trusted both. The voyageurs of the title were the French-Canadian boatmen of the trade, and the boys apprentice themselves to that hard school. Few period series reward rereading like Reid's.
a-journey-into-the-interior-of-the-earth: Jules Verne's Journey to the Interior of the Earth descends into wonder. Professor Lidenbrock leads his small party down an Icelandic volcano. Amazing prehistoric marvels await them far below. The great adventure that started them all.
apollonius-conic-sections-heath:
Thomas L. Heath published his edition of Apollonius's Conic Sections in 1896. Apollonius of Perga, called the Great Geometer, worked around 200 BCE. His Conics became the definitive ancient work on its subject.

Slice a cone at different angles and the curves appear. Circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas all arise from that single cut. Apollonius worked out their properties in propositions of great difficulty. His names for the curves still serve mathematics today. Kepler's astronomy and Newton's physics later depended on this theory. Heath's translation made the peak of ancient geometry readable in English. Few ancient scientific works waited so long for their full vindication.
beltane-the-smith: Beltane the Smith, Jeffery Farnol's medieval romance. The smith's tale unfolds. This book preserves that adventure. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. The library keeps the document safe.
bennett-deacon-skidmore-s-letters-writte: Deacon Skidmore's letters, written for the columns of The Truth Seeker, by Bennett. The deacon's letters. This book preserves that collection. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
bradford-plymouth:
William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony for most of his life, wrote his history of the plantation between 1630 and 1650. The manuscript stayed in family hands, vanished during the Revolution, and resurfaced in England. It is America's founding memoir.

Bradford tells how the Separatists fled England for Holland, then crossed on the Mayflower in 1620. He describes the first winter's deaths, the treaty with Massasoit, and the colony's slow growth. His plain style carries deep faith and quiet grief. The famous line about one small candle lighting a thousand comes from these pages. The manuscript's return to Massachusetts in 1897 was greeted as a homecoming.
camilla-picture-of-youth: Camilla, picture of youth, by Fanny Burney. The young heroine. This book preserves that novel. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
captain-john-smith: John Smith of Jamestown: soldier, writer, and survivor. His bold, rough life is well told here. America’s first true frontiersman. Boldly drawn and well told, bold and rough, well told here, soldier and writer both.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-arbr: This 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Abbey of Arbroath — the Scottish house of the Declaration of Arbroath — recounts its royal founding and fame. Oswald Hunter-Blair tells its stirring story. A key reference on Scotland's history. Scotland's nobles sealed their famous letter in its chapter house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-murim: This 1913 reference article on Adam of Murimuth — the English chronicler of Edward III's wars. Thomas Walsh follows his annals. Crecy and Calais march through his pages. A canon's view of chivalry's age. His chronicle aids historians still. His work continues Murimuth's earlier chronicle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelard-of-ba: A 1913 entry on Adelard of Bath — the scholar who brought Euclid to the West. William Turner honors his translations. He learned from Arab masters in Spain. England's first man of science. His Euclid taught for centuries. His Quaestiones naturales asked daring questions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aelnoth: This 1913 reference piece on Aelnoth — the Canterbury monk who wrote St. Canute's life. Bernard Ward notes his Danish history. He served kings with his pen. The entry preserves his modest fame. A monk among chroniclers. His Canute vita shaped the Danish chronicles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aldfrith: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Aldfrith — the learned king of Northumbria. John Joseph A'Becket praises his scholarship. He sheltered Bede's teachers and monks. The Irish called him Flann Fina. A king among scholars. His reign was Northumbria's golden age. Bede praised his wise rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anathoth: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Anathoth — Jeremiah's hometown. Edward Arbez tells its story. The prophet's foes plotted in its streets. Its fields were bought as a sign. A village in Judah's tale. Its ruins lie north of Jerusalem. Abiathar was exiled to its fields.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-articles-of-f: This 1913 reference piece on the articles of faith — the truths the Church proposes. John Wynne sets out their binding force. The creeds sum their number. The faithful assent with divine faith. The charter of Catholic belief. Their denial is the heretic's mark.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aseneth: A 1913 entry on Aseneth — the wife of Joseph in Egypt. A.E. Breen tells her scriptural story. Pharaoh gave her to the dreamer. Her sons became the tribes. A matriarch of the Egyptian sojourn. Her story inspired the ancient romances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beroth: A 1913 entry on Beroth — Beeroth, the Gibeonite city. John Francis Fenlon notes its scriptural tale. Its men tricked Joshua's oath. The tribe kept its crafty league. A city of the Hivite league. Its water pits gave the name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-judit: This 1913 reference article on the Book of Judith — the widow's triumph. Hugh Pope defends its sacred history. Her dagger freed the besieged town. The Church reads it as God's providence. The deuterocanonical tale of courage. Her song crowns the victory's tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-ruth: This 1913 reference article on the Book of Ruth — the Moabitess's loyal love. Francis Gigot honors its gentle story. Where thou goest, I will go. The great-grandmother of King David. The idyll of the harvest field. Her gleaning won the kinsman's heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corinth: A 1913 entry on Corinth — the Achaean city, now a titular see. Sophrone Pétridès notes its apostolic fame. Paul wrote its famous epistles. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the isthmus' shore. Its Acrocorinth crowns the isthmus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dance-of-deat: A 1913 entry on the Dance of Death — the medieval moral pageant. George Williamson unfolds its grinning tale. The skeleton leads the pope and peasant. The church walls bore the painted round. The memento of the fleeting life. Its Holbein woodcuts are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diemoth: This 1913 reference article on Diemoth — the recluse of Wessobrunn. Michael Ott honors her holy cell. Her pen copied the sacred books. The monks prized their pious sister. The anchoress of the Bavarian abbey. Her Wessobrunn cell is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duluth: This 1913 reference article on Duluth — the Minnesota diocese. Thomas Meehan tells its lake story. Its bishops serve the Superior's shore. The entry traces the young see. A diocese of the northern port. Its Aerial Lift Bridge is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-meredi: A 1913 entry on Edward Meredith — an English martyr of note. Andrew MacErlean honors his blessed death. He died for the Catholic faith. The entry preserves his modest fame. A martyr of the penal age. His 1588 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth: This 1913 reference piece on Elizabeth — the Baptist's mother. Charles Souvay unfolds her scriptural tale. The angel hailed the aged mother. The Magnificat crowned the joyful meeting. The kinswoman of the Virgin Mary. Her Luke tale is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faith: This 1913 reference article on faith — the theological virtue. Hugh Pope unfolds its sublime nature. The mind assents to the revealed truth. The will commands the firm belief. The foundation of the Christian life. Its Hebrews text is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-blyth: This 1913 reference article on Francis Blyth — the Carmelite writer. Benedict Zimmerman notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seventeenth century. A friar among the controversialists. His 1672 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-cha: A 1913 entry on Frederick Husenbeth — the English priest. Oswald Hunter-Blair notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Victorian age. A writer among the clergy. His 1872 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genesareth: A 1913 entry on Genesareth — the Sea of Galilee. The entry gives its scriptural fame. The Lord walked the quiet waves. The fishers left their laden nets. The lake of the Gospel's miracles. Its Gennesaret is the Gospel lake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-m: A 1913 entry on Geoffrey of Monmouth — the British chronicler. Edwin Burton honors his famous Historia. His pen enthroned the Arthurian kings. The bards bless the daring tale. The Homer of the British legends. His 1155 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good-faith: This 1913 reference article on good faith — the honest conscience. Joseph Delany unfolds its legal kinds. The possessor keeps the seemly fruits. The law guards the upright heart. The bona fides of the moralists. Its Roman law is famed.

life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
John Lothrop Motley wrote this history of John of Barneveld, Holland's Advocate. The opening volume covers 1609, as the Twelve Years' Truce began. Motley treats the work as a sequel to his histories of the Netherlands. He also meant it as an introduction to the Thirty Years' War.

His preface argues the Dutch and German wars formed one long tragedy. Eighty years of struggle linked Holland's freedom with Germany's breakup. Barneveld directed Dutch councils through the uneasy pause in fighting. The volume sets his career inside the gathering European storm. The truce with Spain frames every council scene that follows in the volume.
life-of-adam-smith:
John Rae published this life of Adam Smith with Macmillan in 1895. Early chapters cover Smith's early days at Kirkcaldy, his birthplace. His father died young, and his mother raised the future economist. The burgh school and its schoolmaster's drama shape his boyhood.

Smith then studies at Glasgow under Simson and Hutcheson. Hutcheson's economic teaching and influence receive close attention. A Snell exhibition carries Smith on to Oxford and Balliol College. Rae questions Oxford's learning while noting Smith's gratitude to it. Smith's taste for mathematics showed early at Glasgow College. His early connection with David Hume also begins during those years.
light-life-and-love-selections-from-the-:
W. R. Inge selected these writings from medieval German mystics. London's second edition appeared in 1919. Contents name Eckhart first, then Tauler and Suso. Ruysbroek and the Theologia Germanica complete the gathering.

Inge argues the Imitation of Christ came late in the movement. Thomas a Kempis merely toned down Eckhart's characteristic doctrines. True strength lies a full hundred years earlier, he writes. The thirteenth-century awakening, with Francis and Dominic, frames the selections. Meditations on the Seven Words from the Cross join the contents. Bonaventura and Aquinas frame the age Inge calls chivalrous in religion.
lilith:
George MacDonald, a Scots priest and poet, wrote this dark tale for grown readers in 1895. It stands by Phantastes as one of the two peaks of his work. MacDonald wrote late in life, and the book bears the weight of his thought on death.

A man finds a gate in his house to a world of shade and strange laws. There he meets Lilith, the first wife of Adam in old lore, fair and dread at once. The dream walk through that world is a quest for rest, for the dead and the living both.
liza-of-lambeth:
W. Somerset Maugham first published this novel with Heinemann in 1897. It opens on the first Saturday afternoon in August. Broiling heat gives way to a cooler evening in Lambeth. Everyone on Vere Street has come outdoors to enjoy it.

Forty houses face forty identical houses across the street. Dingy grey brick and slate roofs repeat without variation. Children claim the cemented street for noisy cricket games. Coats serve as wickets, and rags or tennis balls fly. Bundles of rags or old tennis balls served the cricketers. Eighty houses matched one another more closely than peas, Maugham writes.
louis-agassiz-as-a-teacher-illustrative-:
Louis Agassiz as a Teacher gathers extracts that show how the great naturalist taught. Lane Cooper, a Cornell professor of English, chose the pieces and wrote the notes. A poem by Lowell opens the book, praising eyes trained to truth. Cooper says his own teaching follows Agassiz's method in essence.

The extracts let students and colleagues tell how Agassiz made them learn. His way was to set the thing itself before the student and demand close looking. Fish, fossils, and shells became teachers in his hands. The book is short but full of wisdom on real study. Teachers of any subject can profit from its pages.
lyrics-of-earth:
Lyrics of Earth is a book of nature poems by Archibald Lampman. Copeland and Day published it at Boston in 1895. Lampman was a Canadian civil servant who wrote in his spare hours. Titles here include 'The Sweetness of Life' and 'April in the Hills.'

'Forest Moods,' 'The Meadow,' and 'In May' show his true subjects. He watches snow, returning seasons, and quiet fields with a painter's eye. His verse is calm, clear, and full of Canadian light. Lampman died young, but his work lived on at home. Many call him the finest nature poet Canada has produced. These lyrics show why that praise endures.
macbeth:
Macbeth is William Shakespeare's tragedy of ambition and murder. Its scenes move from a heath near Forres to Macbeth's castle at Inverness. Three witches greet Macbeth and Banquo with strange prophecies. Lady Macbeth steels her husband to kill King Duncan in his sleep.

The crown won by murder brings no peace to either of them. A banquet is haunted by Banquo's ghost in the room of state. The witches' cauldron brews fresh riddles in a dark cave. Macduff's family is slaughtered at Fife, and revenge gathers in England. At Dunsinane a moving wood fulfills the prophecy at last. It is Shakespeare's shortest and most terrible tragedy.
manhood-perfectly-restored-prof-jean-civ:
Manhood Perfectly Restored is an advertising tract for the Civiale Remedial Agency. The agency sold from 174 Fulton Street, New York. Its remedy was Professor Jean Civiale's soluble urethral crayons. The pamphlet calls them a quick, painless, and certain cure for impotence.

Lost manhood, nervous debility, and kindred troubles fill its list. The cover was sent sealed, and only when requested. Bold type claims official recognition and hospital adoption. Such claims were the stock style of mail-order medicine sellers. The tract survives as evidence of nineteenth-century medical marketing. It shows how shame and hope were used to sell cures.
many-thoughts-of-many-minds-a-treasury-o:
Many Thoughts of Many Minds is a treasury of quotations from all lands and ages. Louis Klopsch compiled it for the Christian Herald in 1896. His preface counts nearly four hundred subjects in the small volume. Upwards of twenty-five hundred extracts fill its pages.

The passages come from standard authors of recognized ability. They are arranged by topic, to serve the largest circle of readers. Preachers, speakers, and writers mined such books for gems. A apt line could crown a sermon or a speech. Klopsch hoped his treasury would help all who received it. The book preserves what one age found worth quoting. It is a compact storehouse of received wisdom.
memoir-correspondence-and-miscellanies-f:
Thomas Jefferson Randolph edited Jefferson's papers in a four volume set. Volume two opens with a letter to Richard Henry Lee. Jefferson wrote it from London on April 22, 1786.

He sends a new lamp, bought after a fruitless search in Paris. On trade, he warns that Britain seeks no pact with America at all. No party there, in or out of power, favors such a link, he says. The letters show a envoy at work in goods, trade, and state craft. A steel plate of Jefferson, from a Stuart painting, fronts the set. Such plates mark the 1829 issue of his papers.
mike-and-psmith:
P. G. Wodehouse's school novel sends Mike Jackson to a new school, Sedleigh, in this story first copyrighted in 1909. There Mike meets Psmith, the calm, talkative boy who becomes his closest ally. Chapter titles promise guerrilla warfare, unpleasantness in the small hours, and a fire brigade meeting. A mystery grows around Jellicoe, missing evidence, and a trail of shoes.

Mr. Downing hunts the culprit like a sleuth-hound while Mike receives a secret commission. The plot clears through Adair's methods and ends with peace declared. The final chapter is the cricket match, Sedleigh against Wrykyn. Wodehouse mixes schoolboy crime, sport, and Psmith's unshakable politeness.
minnesota-its-character-and-climate-like:
Ledyard Bill published this guide to Minnesota in 1871. Bill had already written A Winter in Florida. His preface says Minnesota enjoyed a superior reputation for climate, soil, and scenery. He sets out to explain the real grounds of that pre-eminence.

The book sketches other resorts favorable to invalids besides Minnesota. Copious notes on health accompany the travel material. Bill also gives hints to tourists and emigrants planning the journey. In his day, doctors sent consumptive patients west and north for dry air, and such guides shaped where they went. Minnehaha Falls illustrates the scenery he praises.
muir-boyhood-youth:
John Muir published The Story of My Boyhood and Youth in 1913, the year before his death. It recalls his childhood in Scotland and his family's move to a Wisconsin farm in 1849. The wild boyhood, he shows, made the conservationist.

Muir describes a strict father, long farm labor, and the birds and woods he loved in secret. He taught himself math and whittling, carving clocks and clever machines before dawn. The Wisconsin wilderness, with its prairies and marshes, became his first school. Readers of his mountain books will find their roots in these farm chapters. The book ends as he leaves the farm for the wider world.
my-lady-of-the-north:
Randall Parrish calls this Civil War tale the love story of a gray jacket. A dispatch for Longstreet opens the plot. Night rides, unwelcome guests, and struggles in the dark follow. The hero falls into enemy hands more than once.

Chapters bring Sheridan, death sentences, and staff balls. A battle in the Shenandoah anchors the war scenes. Hand-to-hand fights and lost regiments raise the stakes. Parrish was a master of swift historical romance. V1 praised his color and pace. The tale pairs divided loyalties with love, told at a gallop through the war's most storied valley.
my-life-in-the-south:
Jacob Stroyer tells his own life in slavery and war in this book. A new, enlarged edition came out at Salem, Massachusetts, in 1898. John Wright Buckham praises Stroyer's keen memory in a note. He calls the tale touching, thrilling, and trustworthy.

An 1879 note calls it the inside view of slavery itself. It shows how the enslaved felt under the yoke, in their own words. Such study, the note argues, is still needed for justice. Stroyer writes in a simple, direct style. His book stands as firsthand witness, a Black man's own record of bondage, war, and freedom's hard start.
my-year-of-the-war-including-an-account-:
Frederick Palmer, an American reporter at the British front, wrote this war book. Its contents open with praise for the brave Belgian. Mons, Paris, and the chase of Von Kluck follow. Christmas in Belgium comes under German rule.

Later chapters enter winter trenches and the fight at Neuve Chapelle. Palmer rides with the guns and visits a bombing school. The last third tours the Grand Fleet at sea. He boards destroyers, the Inflexible, and the fleet flagship. Submarine hunts close the record. Palmer gives plain, close reporting on the war's first year, by land and sea.
narrative-of-the-voyage-of-h-m-s-rattles:
John MacGillivray, naturalist to the expedition, wrote this voyage account. H.M.S. Rattlesnake sailed under Captain Owen Stanley from 1846 to 1850. The Admiralty sanctioned the book, issued in two volumes in 1852. Surveys in New Guinea and the Louisiade Archipelago fill it.

An added account tells of E. B. Kennedy's Cape York expedition. MacGillivray dedicated the work to Stanley's mother, in her son's memory. Stanley died before the book appeared in print. The Rattlesnake charted reefs and coasts key to Australian trade. Its naturalist's notes on new lands, peoples, and species still serve science and history.
nasa-tm-19640000194-lunar-flight-study-s:
A Marshall Space Flight Center team wrote this volume of the Lunar Flight Study Series. Volume two studies Earth to Moon transits using star position data. The method relies on the best computer program then available. Part two treats the return flight from lunar orbit to Earth.

Catalog notes list what the part computes for the trip home. Trajectory, reentry conditions, and landing site all come under study. Launch settings from the Moon, called injection conditions, are worked out too. A crew returning from the Moon must hit Earth's air at a safe angle. Studies like this one laid the path math Apollo later flew.
nasa-tm-19640023644-some-results-of-rock: Goddard Space Flight Center issued this report in June 1964 on rocket results from the quiet D region. The D region is the lowest layer of the ionosphere, high above Earth. Catalog notes say Nike-Apache sounding rockets measured electron density profiles there on quiet, mid-latitude days. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable body text, so its measured profiles cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660006036-life-in-space-and-hu:
Su-Shu Huang reviews five books together under the heading of life in space and humanity on Earth. The books are by Shapley, who appears twice, by Merrill, by Cameron, and by Sullivan. Their subjects run from stars and galaxies to interstellar communication and the search for other minds. Shapley's two titles are named first in the contents.

Huang groups the review under the astronomer's gift to humanity. He opens with a tale of the Buddha gaining wisdom under a tree. That broad frame suits books that mix astronomy with big human questions. The review preserves how a space scientist read the popular astronomy of his day, and judged its worth for general readers.
nasa-tm-19660009018-boundary-value-probl:
Hugo L Ingram at Marshall applied optimization theory to trajectory problems in this report, and found a boundary value problem at the center. A boundary value problem fixes conditions at two ends, not one. Best-path problems for rockets naturally take that form. The resulting equations are nonlinear, and not all conditions are given at the same point, Ingram notes.

Three practical numerical methods for solving such problems are discussed. The most efficient method is then explained in detail on a sample problem. Ingram adds that the methods fit other boundary value problems too. Trajectory planning for the Saturn program gave this mathematics a direct, daily use at Marshall.
nasa-tm-19660017919-observations-of-the-:
Principal results from an experiment on the IMP-1 satellite, also called Explorer XVIII, are discussed in this Ames report. The experiment studied the solar wind and how it interacts with Earth's magnetic field. Its main aim was to measure the energy and flow traits of the positive ions in the passing plasma. A curved plate electrostatic analyzer did the measuring on board.

The satellite was launched from Cape Kennedy on November 26, 1963. Its orbit was highly stretched, reaching about thirty-one Earth radii out. That path carried the instruments through both calm and disturbed regions. Early solar wind data of this quality shaped the field's first real picture of the wind.
nasa-tm-19660024079-effect-of-target-mat:
Robert G. Thomson and E. T. Kruszewski of NASA's Langley Research Center wrote this paper for the Seventh Hypervelocity Impact Symposium, held in Tampa, Florida, in November 1964. Their subject is what happens when a very fast projectile punches through a thin metal plate. That question matters for spacecraft, which face tiny particles moving at extreme speeds.

The authors study a visco-plastic flow theory. That kind of theory treats the plate metal as a material that flows under sudden, violent stress. They test whether the theory can predict perforation and the ballistic limit of a plate. The ballistic limit is the speed below which a projectile fails to get through. Their work links that limit to the yield strength of the target material.
nasa-tm-19660024129-the-solar-wind-and-i:
Charles P. Sonett, of the Space Sciences Division at NASA's Ames Research Center in California, reviews the solar wind in this paper. The solar wind is a stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun. Sonett focuses on what happens when that stream reaches Earth's magnetic field, the magnetosphere.

He sums up the wind's known properties and discusses the bow shock formed ahead of Earth. He compares the shock's required conditions with evidence from several space probes. The paper stresses the flow behind the shock, plus particle spectra and turbulence in that region. Sonett also warns that analysis of IMP satellite data was still very early.
nasa-tm-19660030632-electrical-maintenan:
W. E. Neisler, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, presented this talk in January 1964. His subject is unglamorous but vital: keeping the electrical systems of a manufacturing engineering laboratory working. The lab's machines built and tested space hardware, so breakdowns cost more than repair bills.

Neisler explains how the maintenance program grew as demands on it increased. Early on, the lab kept stocks of hard-to-get parts plus tubes, resistors, capacitors, and relays. As welding controls and machine tools grew more complex, that stock and the scrutiny of it had to grow too. The talk lays out the program for fellow engineers.
nasa-tm-19660030689-analysis-of-the-cali:
C. W. Murray Jr., of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this analysis in May 1966. Its subject is the calibration testing of the Varian R-20 rubidium frequency standards, highly precise timing devices built for the Apollo program. The tests themselves were run by the Bureau of Standards on three units from Varian Associates of Palo Alto, California.

Murray used least squares fits to describe how each standard's frequency drifted over time against the United States Frequency Standard. Daily readings strayed from their averages in a pattern matching a normal distribution fairly well. He also calculated each unit's drift over a full year. A straight-line fit, he found, predicted performance more steadily than higher-degree curves, staying within a tight tolerance for well over a year.
nasa-tm-19680006170-scale-model-study-of:
John F. Kline and Roy G. Stabe, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, studied swirling gas flow inside a rocket turbine manifold. The turbine drives the fuel pump of the M-1, a huge hydrogen-oxygen engine. Reference tests had shown puzzling pressure differences around its nozzle, blamed on the manifold.

The manifold is a ring-shaped pipe fed by one radial line. Kline and Stabe measured pressures around the ring on a scale model. They also took smoke trace photographs to see the flow. The pattern proved essentially symmetrical about the feedpipe. The pressure variation they mapped explains the nozzle exit patterns seen earlier.
nasa-tm-19680023437-off-design-theoretic:
Gerald A. Kraft and Brent A. Miller of Lewis Research Center calculate off-design performance for three turbofan engines in this 1968 memorandum. The geared-fan turbofans were sized for light subsonic aircraft. Off-design means running away from the exact conditions the engine was designed for.

The three engines came from preliminary exploratory studies, not a systematic parameter sweep. Still, they illustrate several ways to ease two classic problems. One problem is excessive turbine inlet temperature. The other is compressor surge, a dangerous breakdown of smooth airflow. The study used a bypass ratio and fan pressure ratio shared across the designs. Results show how each engine behaves across its operating range.
nasa-tm-19700005731-optimal-transfer-tra:
Rodney Bradford of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this technical memorandum in October 1969. It studies the best paths a spacecraft can take when it leaves an Earth parking orbit. Each path must end by meeting set conditions on the final orbit it reaches.

Bradford works out these transfer paths under several kinds of end conditions, called conic constraints. He also describes changes made to ROBOT, the computer program used for the work. Reports like this one helped planners pick sound flight paths and keep their design tools up to date.
nasa-tm-19700008419-sensing-molecular-we:
Milton J. LeRoy Jr. and Sol H. Gorland of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in January 1970. They tested a fluidic oscillator as a sensor for the molecular weight of gases. A fluidic oscillator has no moving parts and works by switching a jet of gas back and forth.

The team ran tests with simple and complex gases across a wide weight range. For steady flow, the switching rate matched the speed of sound in the gas. Simple gases and complex gases followed the same rule with different constants. The report also covers how pressure drop and temperature change the rate.
nasa-tm-19700026466-analysis-of-fm-degra:
How multipath effects degrade FM radio signals is analyzed in this Apollo internal note, number MSC-EE-R-68-16. It comes from the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. Multipath means a signal reaches the receiver by several paths at once, after bouncing off nearby surfaces, and the copies can partly cancel each other.

The worry was an enclosed chamber like the orbital workshop, where walls sit close on every side. A communications team ran laboratory tests at the frequencies the workshop would use. Their results show spectrum distortion from multipath in the transmitted signal. A trial in a long enclosed tunnel copied workshop conditions, random objects and all, to see the effect at full scale.
nasa-tm-19700030523-cold-air-investigati:
Herman W. Prust Jr., Harold J. Schum, and Edward M. Szanca of the Lewis Research Center ran this turbine study. It is the first part of a cold-air investigation of transpiration-cooled stator blades. In this cooling scheme, air seeps out through the blade to shield it from hot gas.

This part reports the performance of a stator built with discrete holes for the cooling air. The team measured how the ejected coolant changed the stator's mass flow. They also measured its effect on efficiency. Cold-air rigs let engineers test turbine parts safely and cheaply. The results guide the design of cooled blades for real engines.
nasa-tm-19700032784-on-the-sharpness-of-:
John E. Srawley and E. Roberts Jr. of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper with J. L. Swedlow of Carnegie-Mellon University. It compares the sharpness of real cracks with Wells' crack opening displacement, called COD. The COD idea was widely used in British fracture research.

Wells' measure states how far the faces of a crack open under load. For mild overall bending, it ties simply to the force that grows the crack and to the metal's yield strength. The authors weigh this measure against an equivalent elastic crack. That model crack is longer than the real one but matches its near-tip stresses well.
nasa-tm-19710014504-cold-air-investigati:
NASA engineers reported part four of a cold air turbine study in April 1971, as NASA TM X-2176. The test turbine had stator blades cooled by transpiration. Coolant seeped out through a wire mesh shell on each blade. Hot turbine blades need such cooling to survive engine heat. Cold air tests let staff measure performance safely.

The single stage turbine ran across a range of speeds and pressure ratios. One set of runs held the coolant share near three percent of the main flow. Other runs varied coolant from zero to seven percent at design speed. Results were compared with other cooled designs. A plain uncooled turbine served as the yardstick.
nasa-tm-19710027948-implications-of-rego:
Verne R Oberbeck of the Ames Research Center wrote this October 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,089. It weighs what soil depth at the Apollo 16 landing site would mean for the mission. The lunar soil blanket is called regolith. It is built from the spray of countless small impacts. Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 had landed on basalt flows covered with such soil.

Oberbeck used a Monte Carlo impact cratering model to compute soil thickness. For many flat maria areas, its results matched estimates from small crater shapes. Apollo 16 would land in rougher highland terrain. Knowing the likely soil depth guided sampling plans and equipment choices. The paper extends a proven maria method to the new site.
navaho-houses-seventeenth-annual-report-:
Cosmos Mindeleff wrote Navaho Houses for the Bureau of American Ethnology at the Smithsonian. The piece ran in the bureau's seventeenth annual report, for 1895 to 1896. The Government Printing Office in Washington issued the report in 1898, under director J. W. Powell.

Mindeleff studies the homes of the Navaho people as a record of how they lived. Reports like this one filled the bureau's yearly volumes with field studies of native peoples. They paired text with plates and figures drawn from visits and notes. Modern readers use them as early, close records, while also noting the outlook of their time.
no-refuge-but-in-truth:
Goldwin Smith published No Refuge but in Truth at Toronto in 1908, with Wm. Tyrrell and Company. The Sun Printing and Publishing Company held copyright from 1907. Smith's preface says the letters collected here appeared in the New York Sun. He thanks that paper's editor for printing them.

Chapters treat man and his destiny, and new faith linked with old. The scope of evolution, and its limit, get two chapters. Explanations and the immortality of the soul follow. A last chapter asks if a revolution in ethics is coming. Smith, an old man of letters, defends plain truth against easy new creeds.
north-and-south:
Elizabeth Gaskell first published North and South in Household Words in 1854 and 1855, then in volume form in 1855. Her own note says the weekly form forced her to hurry events near the close. For the book she added short passages and several new chapters. She commends the tale, so mended, to the reader's kindness.

The record's summary names Margaret Hale, whose father leaves the Church on a point of conscience. The family moves from comfortable Hampshire to Milton, a northern mill town. Margaret first hates its ugliness, then sees the poverty of its workers. Chapter one, Haste to the Wedding, opens in Harley Street, with her cousin Edith asleep.
on-conducting-u-eber-das-dirigiren-a-tre: Richard Wagner wrote this treatise on conducting classical music. Edward Dannreuther translated it into English. The German title is Ueber das Dirigiren. The hosted sample preserves only the Project Gutenberg header. That header gives the title, author, and translator. It gives no readable text of the treatise itself. The header also notes the work treats style in performing classical music.
one-of-the-28th:
George Alfred Henty published this tale of Waterloo in 1890. A. L. Burt issued the illustrated New York edition. Henty's preface argues that a woman is the real heroine. A boy plays the principal part and faces adventures. Her nerve equals that of men in active warfare, he says.

Catalog notes name Herbert Penfold and young Ralph Conway. Penfold leaves his estate to a lost love's son. His jealous sisters plot to block that plan. Ralph joins the British Army against Napoleon Bonaparte. The 28th Regiment gives the tale its title. Henty praises women's courage in peril at length.
ordnance-instructions-for-the-united-sta: Ordnance Instructions for the United States Navy, in its fourth edition dated 1866, is the service's official manual for naval guns. The Navy Department's Bureau of Ordnance issued it just after the Civil War. The hosted sample shows the title pages and part headings only. Part One covers preparing vessels of war for battle. It also covers the duties of officers and men when at quarters. Part Two treats the equipment and maneuver of boats, and the exercise of boat howitzers. No instructional body text appears in the sample.
organic-syntheses-an-annual-publication-: Chemists swear by Organic Syntheses, the yearly book of lab-tested recipes for making new compounds. Every method is checked by hand before it appears. The lab worker's bible, exact and trusty, and a quiet monument of science.
phil-purcel-the-pig-driver-the-geography:
Phil Purcel, the Pig-Driver appears in Carleton's Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry, with The Geography of an Irish Oath and The Lianhan Shee beside it. Phil, Carleton says, was a singular character, for he never married, and a knave of the first water besides. Yet he was a general favourite.

The secret of his popularity was that he never laughed. His grave face made his feigned simplicity undetectable, and though he never smiled at his own gains, he made others laugh at their losses. Phil was also a miser, says Carleton, which best explains the gravity.
schiller-wallenstein-coleridge-1800-deat:
Part 2 of Coleridge's Wallenstein, The Death of Wallenstein, appeared in 1800, completing his English version of Schiller's drama. Wallenstein, the imperial general in the Thirty Years' War, has dallied too long with treason. In this part the plots close in and the great man falls.

Astrology, omens, and old comrades' doubts surround Wallenstein as the Emperor's agents move against him. His daughter's love and his own pride hasten the end at Eger. Schiller built the fall as both history and tragedy of character. Coleridge's blank verse gave English readers the full force of it, and the translation stands among his best sustained works.
tanakh-jps-1917-ruth: A Moabite widow chooses loyalty over safety: “whither thou goest, I will go.” Ruth follows her mother-in-law Naomi to Bethlehem, gleans in the fields, and marries Boaz — becoming the great-grandmother of King David. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society edition tells the beloved short story in clear English.
the-cloister-and-the-hearth: The Cloister and the Hearth, Charles Reade's novel. Another edition. This book preserves that classic. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-oliver-go: The complete poetical works of Oliver Goldsmith: the Deserted Village entire. The beloved 18th-century poet. Graceful and tender. An English classic, goldsmith's verse complete, graceful and tender, an English classic, Goldsmith, verse, poems, tender.
the-emigrant-mechanic-and-other-tales-in: Thomas Cowherd, a Canadian blacksmith-poet, rhymes tales of emigrant life with songs of the new land. His homely verse speaks for the working settlers. A genuine folk voice from pioneer Ontario. Anvil, farm, and forest ring through the rhymes of this true poet of the people.
the-heart-s-secret-or-the-fortunes-of-a-: The Heart's Secret, or The Fortunes of a Soldier, a story of love and the low. The soldier's heart. This book preserves that novel. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
the-life-crime-and-capture-of-john-wilke: Written within months of Lincoln's assassination, George Alfred Townsend's book is the first full account of the crime and the manhunt. Drawing on his work as a war correspondent, Townsend traces Booth's plot, the murder at Ford's Theatre, and the desperate chase through Maryland and Virginia. History written while the shock was still fresh.
the-lion-of-the-north: The Lion of the North, G. A. Henty's Thirty Years' War tale. Gustavus Adolphus. This book preserves that historical novel. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
the-masque-of-the-red-death: Poe's 1842 tale of Prince Prospero, who walls himself and his courtiers inside an abbey to escape a plague, holding a masked ball while death stalks outside. When a masked figure in red appears, no one can stop him. In a few pages Poe creates the definitive allegory of mortality's revenge on the powerful.
the-rangers-or-the-tory-s-daughter-a-tal: Daniel Pierce Thompson's Revolutionary romance follows the Rangers of the northern frontier — and the Tory's daughter caught between love and loyalty. Set in Vermont's Green Mountains, it blends history with thrilling adventure. A classic of early American historical fiction, full of period spirit.
the-ruins-or-meditation-on-the-revolutio: Volney's 1791 meditation among the ruins of Palmyra: empires rise and fall, and religion has too often been their tool. The Enlightenment's great elegy on human folly, it influenced revolutionaries from Paris to America. Profound, melancholy, and historically momentous.
the-story-of-the-mormons-from-the-date-o: William Alexander Linn's history of the Mormons from their origin: Joseph Smith, polygamy, and Utah. Thorough and critical, it remains a key source. An important American religious history. Linn's history is essential for understanding Utah.
the-story-of-the-treasure-seekers-being-: E. Nesbit's 1899 children's classic about the Bastable children, who launch a series of harebrained schemes to restore the family fortunes. Digging for treasure, being bandits, and rescuing maidens all go comically wrong, narrated by young Oswald with perfect unreliability. Funny and true to childhood, it reinvented the children's novel.
the-tragedy-of-macbeth: Shakespeare's shortest tragedy and his most intense: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth murder their way to the Scottish throne and are destroyed by guilt. Witches, blood that will not wash, and a walking forest drive toward the bleak end. A terrifying study of ambition, and endlessly stageable.
the-underground-city-or-the-black-indies: Jules Verne's 1877 novel of a vast coal mine under Scotland, where miners build a whole underground city. Mystery, engineering marvels, and a touch of the supernatural fill this tribute to Scottish industry. Verne's love letter to the land of his publisher.
the-winning-of-barbara-worth: Harold Bell Wright's bestselling novel follows the winning of Barbara Worth — and the winning of the desert itself through irrigation — in early California. Romance and reclamation blend in a story that celebrated hard work and vision. The hugely popular book that made Wright one of America's best-loved authors.
the-young-voyageurs-boy-hunters-in-the-n: The Young Voyageurs, boy hunters in the north, by Mayne Reid. The northern hunt. This book preserves that adventure. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
travels-in-england-during-the-reign-of-q: Paul Hentzner's travels in Elizabethan England: a German visitor's view of the Virgin Queen's realm. Curious and detailed, it is a priceless outsider's account. Tudor England through foreign eyes. Hentzner's England is Tudor life in miniature.
trials-and-triumphs-of-faith: Mary Cole recounts trials and triumphs of faith — true stories of humble believers tested by sorrow and delivered by grace. Her earnest narratives comforted many Victorian readers. Simple, sincere Christian testimony, warmly told. Sickbeds, losses, and answered prayers fill these earnest pages.
visit-to-iceland-and-the-scandinavian-no: Ida Pfeiffer's 1846 account of her solo journey to Iceland and Scandinavia. The intrepid Viennese widow describes geysers, glaciers, and northern life with fearless curiosity. One of the great Victorian travel books by a woman. Pfeiffer traveled alone where few men dared to go.
westcott-kabir-panth:
G. H. Westcott published Kabir and the Kabir Panth in 1907. His study gives the classic English account of the weaver-saint. Kabir's sect, the Panth that bears his name, fills the second half.

Kabir's verses lash priestcraft in both Hindu and Muslim camps alike. He mocks empty rite and praises the God found in the heart. Westcott traces the saint's life, songs, and the order that spread them. His book rests on texts and talks with Kabir's own followers. Readers meet India's most quoted mystic in a clear, warm, firm guide. Westcott's respect for Kabir's bite keeps the study fresh today.
youth: Tolstoy closes his trilogy with Youth: the hero at the university, proud and lost by turns. His self-lacerating honesty spares nothing. A young genius learning to see himself clear, a young genius seeing himself clear.
